(1) Collective payload per receiver GPU, the ≤ 0.2 gate: 19,653,279,744 / 134,157,778,944 = 0.1465 in all 20 publications for all 8 receivers (the candidate's eight receiver values are identical in every publication; the reference's equal its wire inventory, 502 entries). (2) Installed bytes: the reference proves 19,687,358,464 B compared per receiver; the candidate's replay compared exactly the prepared installed bytes of every receiver (the collection refuses otherwise), and its payload is 34,078,720 B below the installed count because the router is widened BF16→FP32 on install, not on the wire. (3) Physical ingress on the one declared observer host (`ga8b3d8`, 17 HCA ports deduplicated, the host holding all eight receivers): 135.54 GB per publication in the candidate against 135.69 GB in either reference, ratio 0.9989; the candidate's per-publication sum of policy logical root injection is 134,157,778,944 B, the reference's full wire size. The physical counter is a reported quantity and not a gate (root's correction: a reference node receives one copy and fans out locally); it is reported here because the per-GPU payload cut does not show up as a host-level wire cut in this geometry, and that should be read, not assumed away. One arithmetic fact bounds it: all eight receivers live on that one host, and the host's ingress in both arms equals the model's wire size (134,157,778,944 B) to within 1.1%, so in this geometry every byte of the update enters the receiver host once either way and no host-level byte cut is possible; the 39× time cut is therefore not fewer host bytes but a shorter path for the same bytes (32 sources streaming to 8 receivers in parallel instead of one root's broadcast). Where exactly they enter is not shown by these counters.

Identity evidence. Candidate: `K10_TWENTY_PUBLICATION_AUDIT_PASS`, publications 1-20 on one manifest `6395bf27`, five original attempts (`72764b28`, `72c47cc5`, `8e355046`, `945a20b4`, `b828a04e`), marker attempt `945a20b4`, 3,554 readback objects, no host mixing policy and receiver ranks; every receiver's replay row asserted at mismatches 0, coverage 1, compared = expected (`l0-k10-v2-native-reducer.py:99`; policy source proof `:89`; core `installed_replay`). Reference a4: `K10_REFERENCE_TWENTY_BYTE_PHYSICAL_AUDIT_PASS` wrapping `K8_20_SYNC_PERSISTED_BYTE_MEMORY_IDENTITY_PASS`, 20 syncs, 158 buckets, five originals, marker `0b780d86`, 3,553 objects, receiver replay peak extra ≤ 852,480 B. Reference a3: same pass lines on `c7cea14b`, marker `5559f3ad`.

**What this means.** The P32/I8 gate row passes on both of its declared conditions: p50 install 0.5088 s ≤ 4 s (and below the 1.5 s stretch on both readings, 0.51 s and 1.25 s), and per-receiver collective payload 0.1465 ≤ 0.2, with a zero-mismatch full-byte proof on all twenty publications of both arms. Against the matched reference on the same runtime the timed interval is 39× shorter and the conservative interval 16× shorter, both far beyond the ≥ 4× the milestone asks for. Decision: the expert-block transport is kept for this geometry.
What it does not say. The milestone "weight sync cut ≥ 4×" is about the whole weight-sync interval in a training run, and this pair measures one update's transfer-and-install with the gate-only proofs on (about 26 s of proof per publication that production will not run) and the outer pause/drain/resume unmeasured in both arms; the run-level interval with proofs off is a separate measurement. The gate matrix has two more required rows, P32/I16 and P16/I24 (the latter needs the class-T precision package), before the milestone is declared. The observer-host ingress is unchanged between arms; the design says that is expected of a fan-out and makes the per-GPU payload the gate, but nobody has yet shown where the candidate's bytes enter the receiver host, and I am not guessing. Within-run spread: candidate install max 0.858 s (three publications above 0.75 s), reference a4 max 24.33 s at publication 16; neither is out of line with the a3 rows, so no rerun is called for under the pairing rule. Runtime envelope: the a4 pair exists because the a3 candidate wrote its shard receipts to a pod-local path (`/app/marinskyrl/s3:/…`, a launcher path heuristic), so its collection could not run; `c7cea14b → 501216e2` changes only `cloud/iris/paths.py` and its test (29 insertions, nothing under `skyrl_train/`), so the measured runtime is byte-identical, but because that file is in the packet's hashed source set the packet (`dede2213 → fcffca0a`) and preparation (`0ddc94fc → eda658fc`) were re-frozen rather than treated as envelope; the a3 reference is therefore a same-code, different-hash row, which is why the a4 reference was run and is the pin.

**Next.** Run the P32/I16 row (packet pending its first pair) and the P16/I24 row once the class-T precision package is composed and the node-placement precondition (K26) holds; measure a run-level weight-sync interval with the proofs off; then the milestone comment "weight sync cut ≥ 4× with bit-identical proof".

**What we did and why.** This is the second row of the K10 gate matrix, following the P32/I8 row (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5634012950): same 32 policy ranks, twice the inference side (16 receivers, two node-local vLLM replicas of DP8/EP8 on two hosts), same runtime `501216e2`, frozen packet `191916dd`, preparation `e35be532`, twenty measured publications per arm, candidate (shard mode) and matched reference (original loader, physical counters on) launched together. The question the row answers is whether the expert-block transport's per-receiver payload and install time hold when the receiver count doubles, or whether the second replica pays a second broadcast. Each arm was read by an independent CPU collection binding original attempt identity, the one-shot marker, the full object catalogue and, for the candidate, every receiver's stream rows against the prepared schedule; the paired numbers are recomputed from the two audit JSONs only, by a reducer that reads the geometry from the JSONs and asserts the node/receiver identities (it reproduces the posted P32/I8 line field for field).

**What is timed, exactly.** As in the P32/I8 comment: the candidate's gate number is the `install` phase (driver wall around the concurrent `run_shard_publication` on policy ranks and `run_shard_stream` on receivers, `shard_interval.py:151-153`, equal to the driver's `timing/weight_broadcast`); `freeze`, `receiver_begin` and `finish` are production phases timed separately and added in the conservative reading; `source_replica_proof` and `full_byte_replay` are gate-only proofs excluded from every timed reading; counter reads sit outside the install wall. The reference's number is the per-policy-rank wall of the original loader through `cuda.synchronize` and a barrier (`bucket_timing_session.py:295-301`), max over the 32 ranks per sync. 🤖 E7.1 precision fleet, 33 arm-seeds audited: on Megatron, fp32 optimizer state (+4.95 pp) and bf16 moments at 100 updates (+4.17 pp) beat the native control beyond the 2 pp margin, bf16 gradient reduce is neutral (+0.91 pp), 16-bit remainders (−3.91 pp) and bf16 moments run to 300 updates (−13.80 pp) are worse; every difference lives in the completion channel, not in answer content; the FSDP2 half is too seed-volatile to carry a lever claim

**What we did and why.** The precision levers that make Snowball training cheaper (bf16 optimizer moments, bf16 gradient reduction, 16-bit parameter remainders, stochastic or Kahan rounding) are only worth carrying if they leave answer quality alone. E7.1 screens them on Qwen3-0.6B before any Snowball run pays for them: eleven arms, three seeds each (17, 29, 43), 16 H100 per arm-seed on RNO, objective `behavior_clip` (PLAN-SPEC §4.1 Bucket S), the PLAN-SPEC §4.2 quality contract read at every eval point (updates 0, 20, …, 100; sixteen points for the 300-update arms), 256 questions per point. Six Megatron families paired against the native control (`mega-native`, fp32 everything): `mega-aware-fp32` (the precision-aware kernel with fp32 state, the L3 control), `mega-bf16-both-100` and `-300` (bf16 m and v, the latter run to 300 updates so the β₂ warm-up completes), `mega-bf16-grad-reduce` (L2), `mega-fp32-remainders` (L4a). Five FSDP2 families paired against their own control per the manifest's pass line (`fsdp2-fp32master-fp32`; a cross-backend delta would confound lever with backend): `fsdp2-fp32master-bf16` (L2 in FSDP2 form), `fsdp2-stochastic-fp32` (L3+L4b), `fsdp2-kahan-fp32` (L4c), `fsdp2-nearest-fp32` (L4d, the positive control expected to freeze). Every arm-seed has a per-arm scientific-audit receipt: W&B history read twice and identical, every row inside the original task interval, the eval dumps proven through the frozen auditor, the contract re-derived per row, and `rewarded-but-truncated == 0` held at every eval point of every arm. Pooled deltas are paired by question at matching seed with a 95% paired-question bootstrap (10,000 draws); the manifest's seed rule refuses any family with fewer than three seeds, and none is refused.

**Repair on the way (directives §4.5).** All fifteen FSDP2 arm-seeds first died seven seconds into the driver: the recipe set `trainer.optimizer_state_metrics=True` unconditionally (`experiments/post_training/async_rl.py:511`) and SkyRL's validator refuses it off Megatron (`skyrl_train/utils/utils.py:612`; the observer exists only in `megatron_worker.py:503`). The manifest's own limitation note had called the flag a no-op on FSDP2; it is a hard launch failure. Repaired with a compose-time guard and a cross-product test (marin `a453edb9`), and the fifteen FSDP2 arm-seeds recomposed without the flag as manifest v3 (`b71195a5`; the eighteen Megatron entries byte-identical to v2 `01c9165a`; `validate_cfg` accepts all fifteen recomposed configs and rejects all fifteen v2 ones). The failed v2 runs consumed no measurement guard. One arm-seed, `fsdp2-stochastic-fp32-seed29`, completed its run but its coordinator was killed by hand after a worker preemption 50 s after the head published its result left the gang unable to reschedule; its receipt is audited under a named exception (see the footnote) and is admitted to the pool explicitly.

Truncation fraction at the final point, per seed: the two collapsing Megatron arms are `mega-fp32-remainders` seed 17 (52%; its seeds 29 and 43 sit at 12% and 10%) and `mega-bf16-both-300` seed 17 (80% at update 300; 14% and 33% at the other seeds); the native seed-17 control itself truncates 30%. FSDP2 truncation ranges from 5% (`nearest`, all seeds) to 91% (the FSDP2 control at seed 29).

Semantic score (answer content, over resolved rows, 180–254 of 256 per family) is flat across every family, 65–75%, and sits above the contract everywhere: Megatron 71.6–75.5%, FSDP2 65.5–73.9%. The contract differences above are therefore differences in how many answers reach a complete, well-formed stop, not in whether the model solved the problem.

**What this means.** On Megatron the screen is clean: fp32 optimizer state in the precision-aware kernel and bf16 moments at 100 updates both beat the native control beyond the margin with tight intervals; bf16 gradient reduction is neutral and can be carried for free (it is the lever the K10 P16 memory repair now leans on); exact 16-bit remainders and bf16 moments run to 300 updates are worse, in both cases through one seed collapsing into truncation while the other two seeds are level with or above the control, so the loss is a stability loss, not a capacity loss, and it is not a licence to run bf16 moments long. On FSDP2 the intervals exclude zero for four levers, but the reading must stop there: the bootstrap resamples questions at fixed seeds and carries no seed-to-seed variance, and the FSDP2 seed spread is enormous (the FSDP2 control ranges from 5% to 70% completed across seeds; `fsdp2-fp32master-bf16` runs −9, +37 and −52 pp across its three seeds). Those intervals say the questions separate the arms at these seeds; they do not license a lever claim, and the `stochastic` verdict rests on seed 29, the exception seed. The `nearest` positive control did not freeze on this contract; whether it froze at the parameter level cannot be read, because the changed-element probe rejects FSDP2 (`weight_change_probe.py:371-377`). Not measured here, from the manifest's pass line: grad-norm divergence at equal seed and order, m/v relative error at updates 1/10/100, the update-10 bitwise check of `mega-fp32-remainders` against `mega-aware-fp32`, and the changed-element fraction; the first three need the Megatron optimizer-state receipts read by a collector that does not yet exist, the last has no emitter on either backend. Tokens and core-seconds columns are absent because the synchronous runner logs no `async/performance/*` keys.

**Next.** Read the Megatron optimizer-state receipts for the m/v error and the update-10 bitwise check; carry `bf16_grad_reduce` into the K10 P16 memory repair; do not carry `fp32_remainders` or long bf16 moments to Snowball without a stability run; treat the FSDP2 half as a seed-volatility finding about the FSDP2 recipe at this scale rather than as lever evidence.

[^exc]: `fsdp2-stochastic-fp32-seed29` was audited under the `terminal_manifest_absent` variant: its head task succeeded and published the result at 12:24:19 UTC, the worker acknowledged it at 12:24:20 and was deleted by the scheduler at 12:25:10; the coordinator, unable to see the gang finish, was cancelled by hand and never wrote its terminal manifest, so eight coordinator-attestation checks (`gate_return_identity`, `gate_return_child`, `child_job_name`, `coordinator_response_digest`, `coordinator_response_join`, `terminal_request`, `terminal_response`, `terminal_response_identity`) are replaced by the durable training receipt's request fingerprint recomputed from the frozen envelope (exact match), the measurement guard claimed by the head task's original attempt, and the a2 relaunch's own refusal (`Existing measured output …`), all quoted in the receipt. The receipt lives in a separate namespace (`scientific-audit-v2-exception/`) and the pool admits it only under an explicit flag.

comments.body:
🤖 E5.2 Qwen throughput matching, three arms: the λ_I(c) fit is degenerate and the T_step prediction misses by 29–38% on every arm, because no arm was generation-bound and the generation-workers knob did not move per-engine concurrency (measured 12.4 / 5.5 / 5.1 running requests per engine against nominal 32 / 64 / 128)

**What we did and why.** E5.2 fits the inference throughput curve λ_I(c) = λ_max·c/(c+c_half) from three runs at different generation-worker counts, reads the learner rate λ_L from `run_training`, and predicts the step time; the done-when is a prediction within 15% and a recommended P:I per rung. Three Qwen3-0.6B arms on RNO, 16 H100 each (P8 TP2 + I8 TP1), staleness 3, K=1, workers 64 / 128 / 256 (nominal 32 / 64 / 128 per engine), N2 × 8 steps (16 optimizer updates), seed 17, objective `behavior_clip`, eval at 0 and 8, one W&B step per optimizer update (MSR `fully_async_trainer.py:539,661`). The collector binds each run by job name from its coordinator's training-return line, reads its history twice in a CPU pod, checks every required key, and fits from the cohort-level sums (core seconds, consumed tokens, publish time) with the per-update learner time taken from `run_training` directly.

**Results.** All three arms ran to completion (6 native tasks, zero failures); `rejected_rate` 0 and `buffer_wait_fraction` 0.001–0.004 on every arm, so the learner never waited for generation.

| arm | c nominal | c measured (median running reqs/engine) | λ_I point (tok/s/GPU) | λ_L per optimizer update (tok/s/GPU) | L per cohort | T_step predicted | T_step measured | error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| w64 | 32 | 12.4 | 852.9 | 1523 | 109,788 | 21.2 s | 15.4 s | +37.7% |
| w128 | 64 | 5.5 | 1005.1 | 1324 | 109,682 | 21.2 s | 16.0 s | +32.6% |
| w256 | 128 | 5.1 | 1050.0 | 1288 | 101,417 | 19.7 s | 15.3 s | +28.7% |

Fit: λ_max = 718.7 tok/s/GPU, c_half = 0.0 (the three points show throughput falling with nominal c; residuals −16 / −28 / −32%). `E52_QWEN_THROUGHPUT_FIT_FAIL arms=3 tstep_within_15pct=0/3`. The measured cohort time is identical across arms (15.3–16.0 s) and is explained by the learner side alone: two `run_training` calls of about 4.8 s, about 2.1 s publish, about 3.5 s cohort preparation (old-logprob and reference forwards on the opening step). The balance table the collector prints (I = 16 "balanced") inherits the degenerate curve and is not a recommendation.

**What this means.** The done-when is not met, and the cause is the measurement, not the collector: (1) the λ_I points are idle-engine readings, not capacity readings, because at I=8 with this cohort the arms are learner-bound, and the brief's own condition for the throughput metric to equal capacity (generation-bound) never held; (2) the generation-workers knob is not the concurrency lever the design assumed: per-engine running requests fell as workers rose, so either the buffer never filled in four cohorts or the workers setting bounds something other than in-flight requests per engine, which has to be read from the recipe before any re-run. No P:I recommendation is issued from this group. The Snowball repeat stays gated on K10 as before.

**Next.** One of: (a) a longer run (16–32 cohorts) so the buffer reaches steady concurrency; (b) a generation-bound arm, by a larger cohort at I=8 or by I=4 (which needs the recipe's I ∈ {8, 16} restriction relaxed and a topology ruling); (c) capacity read from `vllm/peak_running_reqs` windows instead of medians. Before any of them: trace what `--generation-workers` actually bounds at MSR 65fa9170 and state the real per-engine concurrency lever.

🤖 E7.1 addendum: the three owed pass-line items read from the Megatron optimizer-state receipts — the grad-norm divergence criterion does not discriminate levers at this scale (the fp32-state control itself diverges 90–210% from the native control through rollout sampling variance), and the m/v relative error and the update-10 bitwise remainders check have no emitter at MSR 65fa9170

**What we did.** A collector read, for each of the 18 Megatron arm-seeds, the per-update raw gradient norm (`policy/by_update/{i}/raw_grad_norm`, W&B and Finelog agreeing on every update) and the once-per-rank optimizer-state inventory (`optimizer_state_storage`/`_settings`/`_inventory`, 8 policy ranks per arm), bound to the same run identities as the posted audit (job `/atqamar/async-rl-v2-e71-optimizer-state-v1-2`; the first attempt returned no rows because the Finelog `cluster` column is null on cw-rno2a rows, the same trap K10 hit). Equal order was verified per pair by the consumed-uid digest being identical on every step.

**Results.** Grad-norm divergence, defined as the maximum over paired updates of |g_lever(u) − g_native(u)| / g_native(u) at equal seed, against the manifest's "< 1%" line:

| family | divergence max, seeds 17 / 29 / 43 | at update 1 | at update 10 | at update 100 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| mega-aware-fp32 (fp32 state, L3 control) | 2.11 / 0.90 / 1.74 | 0.072 / 0.019 / 0.012 | 0.47 / 0.18 / 1.65 | 0.45 / 0.21 / 0.38 |
| mega-bf16-both-100 | 1.75 / 2.97 / 0.91 | 0.090 / 0 / 0.045 | 0.14 / 0.24 / 0.013 | 0.45 / 0.10 / 0.31 |
| mega-bf16-both-300 | 2.59 / 1.64 / 1.99 | 0.072 / 0.012 / 0.048 | 0.055 / 0.11 / 0.020 | 0.010 / 0.17 / 0.34 |
| mega-bf16-grad-reduce | 0.87 / 1.53 / 0.67 | 0.018 / 0.013 / 8e-5 | 0.23 / 0.50 / 0.19 | 0.51 / 0.16 / 0.016 |
| mega-fp32-remainders | 1.23 / 2.54 / 1.57 | 0.058 / 0.019 / 0.002 | 0.34 / 0.15 / 0.95 | 0.004 / 0.37 / 0.39 |

Every arm-seed fails the 1% line, including the control that differs from native only by kernel. Medians over updates are 0.13–0.17 for every family. Optimizer-state bytes per parameter from the inventories: 12.0 (native, aware-fp32, grad-reduce), 10.0 (remainders, int16 master), 8.0 (bf16 moments); owned elements 596,115,456 per rank.

**What this means.** The divergence criterion as written measures rollout sampling variance, not the precision lever: once two runs draw different samples at update 1 (the aware-fp32 control is already 1.2–7.2% off at u=1 and 18–165% off by u=10), gradient norms decorrelate regardless of precision, so no arm can pass and no arm's failure says anything about its lever. The two remaining items cannot be measured from these runs: the optimizer-state observer emits byte and dtype inventories once after the first update (`optimizer_state_metrics.py:181-247`) and never the moment values needed for an m/v relative error, and nothing exports or digests parameters at update 10 (`ckpt_interval=-1`, `hf_save_interval=-1`, no digest emitter), so the remainders-vs-aware bitwise check has no operand; the closest available reading, the grad-norm deviation at u=10 (0.089 / 0.020 / 0.262 by seed), is not identical through u ≤ 10 on any seed and is not a bitwise check. The quality verdicts of the group comment stand as posted; these three items are struck from the pass line as unmeasurable or non-discriminating at this runtime, and the instrumentation gaps are logged for the runtime lane.

**Next.** If a precision-level check is still wanted: a same-sample replay (fixed rollouts) for the divergence item, an m/v error emitter at updates 1/10/100, and a parameter digest at a named update; none exists today.

🤖 E5.2 v3, four arms with the buffer lever set: the step-time prediction lands within 15% on all four arms at their realised operating points, but realised concurrency stays at 5–9 requests per engine whatever the workers setting, because the closed loop is learner-rate-limited (Little's law reproduces every arm with no free parameter); the λ_I(c) curve is not measurable inside this trainer at I=8 with a 0.6B policy and needs a standalone engine benchmark

**What we did and why.** After the first E5.2 group (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5638763417) a code trace showed that `--generation-workers` also sets the completed-output buffer depth, so raising it parked finished groups against the staleness budget. v3 fixed that with `++trainer.fully_async.max_buffered_groups=64` on every arm (the override reaches the composed config and is asserted on it) and ran W = 64 / 128 / 256 as λ_I points plus one arm at W=256 with `--max-num-seqs 16` intended as a generation-bound capacity reading. Same geometry as before: Qwen3-0.6B, P8 TP2 + I8 TP1 on RNO, staleness 3, K=1, N2 × 8 steps, seed 17, `behavior_clip`; the capped arm enters the analysis only as a consistency check against the fitted curve.

**Results.** All four arms completed. Per arm at the realised concurrency c (median running requests per engine):

| arm | W | max_num_seqs | c realised | groups in flight | T_L | T_I (fitted) | T_step predicted | T_step measured | error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| w64-b64 | 64 | 1024 | 7.0 | 14 | 8.99 s | 12.36 s | 14.39 s | 14.90 s | −3.4% |
| w128-b64 | 128 | 1024 | 9.0 | 18 | 10.30 s | 11.27 s | 13.37 s | 15.49 s | −13.7% |
| w256-b64 | 256 | 1024 | 5.06 | 10 | 10.34 s | 14.80 s | 16.84 s | 15.46 s | +8.9% |
| w256-b64-s16 | 256 | 16 | 7.69 | 15 | 11.12 s | 12.98 s | 15.05 s | 16.32 s | −7.8% |

Fit over the three uncapped arms: λ_max = 2575.8 tok/s/GPU, c_half = 9.55, residuals +21% / −7% / −10%; the capped arm's own reading (1074.8 tok/s/GPU at c = 7.7) sits 6.9% from the curve. `E52_QWEN_THROUGHPUT_FIT_FAIL arms=4 tstep_within_15pct=4/4 … coverage_ok=False`: the collector's coverage gate (realised c within 25% of nominal) fails on every arm (0.22 / 0.14 / 0.04 of nominal), and that gate is the honest verdict.

**What this means.** Every candidate cap is slack: the staleness budget re-derived with the real keys allows 256 generating groups (128 sequences per engine, exactly `max_num_seqs`), admission drains the whole queue on cohort-opening steps, the buffer plus parked workers hold a full cohort at every drain (hence `buffer_wait_fraction ≈ 0`), and the dataloader gates nothing. What fixes the in-flight count is the learner's drain rate: N = λ_L·P / r × duty (r the per-sequence decode rate, duty = 1 − 2·t_pub/T) predicts 68 / 54 / 38 / 54 sequences in flight against the measured 56 / 72 / 41 / 62, with no free parameter and the right ordering, and it contains no W, buffer or staleness term. So the four "points" sit in a band the knob does not set, c_half is noise, the balance table beyond c ≈ 9 is an extrapolation, and the capped arm never became generation-bound because 16 is already above what the flow needs. The done-when's prediction criterion holds at the realised operating point (all four within 15%), which says the T_step model is right where it was measured, not that a P:I recommendation exists: a larger cohort is neutral (the drain rate does not move), a slower learner moves the wrong way. No P:I recommendation is issued from this group either; the Snowball repeat stays gated on K10.

**Next.** Measure λ_I(c) with a standalone vLLM concurrency benchmark against the same eight engines, model and sampling parameters (outside the trainer's closed loop), then re-run the T_step prediction with that curve; read `vllm/peak_running_reqs` once to settle burst-versus-steady for the record. Nothing in the trainer's own metrics can give the curve at this scale.

comments.body:
🤖 K18-D1 native gate: the D1 candidate fails both operands as written, and the second failure is the informative one — under the gate's own geometry no rollout was ever aborted at a weight sync (abort count 0 on every step, version spread 0 on every update), so the per-token version tags D1 adds had nothing to tag; the reward-band operand also fails, but a min/max band of three controls passes an identical run only 6% of the time over four cohorts

**What we did and why.** K18-D1 carries per-token policy-version tags through the existing abort-and-resubmit partial-rollout path, so that a group whose generation straddles a weight sync records which tokens came from which policy version. Shared promotion of D1 was gated on a native run: Qwen3-0.6B, C1/A1/N2, eight optimizer updates (four cohorts), P8 TP2 + I8 on RNO, three pre-change controls (seeds 17, 29, 43, control runtime `2750c83f` = shared 65fa9170 plus the staging-retry hunks) and one D1 candidate (seed 17, native runtime `a34d40c5` = control plus the D1 commit, patch-identical to `4a71789c`). The pass line, frozen before the candidate was released: every candidate update's admission reward inside the per-cohort min/max band of the three controls, never widened; at least one consumed update with `async/version_spread_max ≥ 1`; token-age fractions summing to one over the known tokens with coverage stated; schema-4 retained records validating through the frozen reader. Stage 1 froze the band from the three finished controls (identity by completion fingerprint, history read twice) and the candidate was launched bound to the band's digest; stage 2 evaluated it.

**Results.** Candidate `d1-seed17` ran clean (two tasks, one attempt each, zero failures, zero preemptions, on the same two physical nodes as control-seed17).

| cohort (updates) | candidate reward | band [min, max] | controls s17 / s29 / s43 | inside |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (1, 2) | 0.18199 | [−0.00142, 0.15390] | 0.15390 / 0.08841 / −0.00142 | no, above by 0.028 |
| 3 (3, 4) | 0.17302 | [0.18176, 0.20579] | 0.20579 / 0.19019 / 0.18176 | no, below by 0.009 |
| 5 (5, 6) | 0.31926 | [0.27083, 0.29098] | 0.27083 / 0.29086 / 0.29098 | no, above by 0.028 |
| 7 (7, 8) | 0.35091 | [0.34026, 0.39863] | 0.34026 / 0.38976 / 0.39863 | yes |

Version evidence, all eight updates: `async/version_spread_max` = 0 (mean 0); `async/staleness_newest_mean` 0, 1, 0.25, 1.19, 0.5, 1.5, 0.31, 1.25; `async/token_age_frac/{0,1,2,3plus}` sum to 1.0 at every update with `known_token_fraction` 1.0 (431,727 known loss tokens, 0 unknown) and complete-group fraction 1.0; `response_abort_count` = 0 at every step with abort-evidence fraction 1.0. Schema-4 retention: 188 archives, 297 records, 0 reader errors, 297/297 complete version runs, 0 null abort counts. Staging 6.9–7.7 s per node on all four arms. `K18_D1_GATE_FAIL reason=reward_outside_band`; the frozen reader's `validate_consumed_versions` raises `No consumed mixed-version evidence` independently.

**What this means.** Two separate things. First, the gate's geometry never exercised the code D1 changes: with C1/A1 and these response lengths, no in-flight rollout straddled a weight sync, the abort-and-resubmit path fired zero times, every consumed group carried a single policy version, and the tags were all trivially correct; the age fractions and the schema-4 records show the plumbing works end to end (known-token coverage 1.0, complete version runs on every record) but say nothing about mixed-version groups, which is what D1 is for. The gate cannot pass as specified until its geometry produces aborts, and that is a design correction, not a D1 defect. Second, the reward-band operand as written has no power at three controls: a null fourth run falls outside a min/max band of three exchangeable samples with probability 2/(n+1) = 1/2 per cohort, so it stays inside all four cohorts with probability 1/16; the candidate's one-of-four inside, missing above at two cohorts and below at one while sharing seed 17 with a control that itself sits at the band edge, is what a null draw looks like. The band was not widened and will not be; what it needs is more controls or an interval rule, which is a ruling above this session. D1 is not promoted by this run; nothing here argues against it either.

**Next.** Re-freeze the gate with a geometry that produces aborts (a sync interval shorter than the generation length, or forced abort at the boundary, so `response_abort_count > 0` and `version_spread_max ≥ 1` are reachable) and a band rule with stated power (more controls, or a tolerance interval) before the candidate is released again; the controls' histories and the candidate's archives are durable and can be reused for any re-analysis that does not change the rule after the fact.

🤖 All 12 correction runs crossed the 0.1-nat entropy stop threshold

**What we did and why.** We compared six off-policy correction methods at two rollout-age settings on Qwen3-0.6B, as a screen for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. The correction comparison (E4.3) is class R: the experiment decides whether any correction qualifies for selection. The first seed ran 96 optimizer updates per configuration, with two disjoint optimizer minibatches per prepared cohort and development evaluation every 32 updates.

**Results.** All 12 runs completed their requested updates, but every configuration crossed the pre-specified policy-entropy stop threshold. Each consumed the same 6,144 prompt groups and 24,576 responses. The 12 conditional second-seed runs are closed without launch because their first-seed configurations failed that scientific gate.

| Correction | Minimum entropy at age setting 1 / 2, nats | Updates below 0.1 at setting 1 / 2, out of 96 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Behavior clipping | 0.071165591 / 0.080584244 | 12 / 7 |
| Regular objective | 0.083199000 / 0.084338995 | 11 / 16 |
| Regular + capped importance sampling | 0.078978268 / 0.087671585 | 13 / 8 |
| Regular + importance-weight mask | 0.074850183 / 0.087887925 | 16 / 5 |
| Behavior clipping + importance-weight mask | 0.089487072 / 0.099840082 | 12 / 1 |
| Regular + M2 objective | 0.060714210 / 0.089728169 | 29 / 5 |

The two age settings produced distinct consumed-group distributions in every correction pair: mean age 0.958333333 versus 2.333333333 optimizer updates, with group-weighted 95th percentiles of 2 versus 3. The entropy measurement is actual policy vocabulary entropy; disabled diagnostic zeros were excluded. The runs continued to update 96 despite the observed stop condition.

Final held-out eight-draw completed correctness, semantic correctness and paired quality confidence intervals remain unavailable for all 12 runs. Native development scores were collected, but have not been joined to the frozen question-level harness evidence and do not support correction ranking. There is no selected correction or demonstrated quality-adjusted speedup.

**What this means.** This comparison concludes with 12 scientific failures and 12 conditional cells closed without launch. No method met the required health criterion, so the current behavior-clipping recipe remains an unselected baseline. The entropy failures prevent a clean correction recommendation; the realised-age separation alone does not establish how much staleness preserves answer quality.

**Next.** Carry the negative correction disposition into the cadence comparison and preserve the retained checkpoints for the outstanding held-out audit. The next correction milestone, “correction chosen and safe-bound rule,” remains incomplete; it must report that no correction qualified under this protocol.

🤖 Optimizer storage halves to 6 bytes per parameter; both 32-GPU learners fit

**What we did and why.** We compared Snowball's native optimizer with bf16 moments and
16-bit parameter remainders to measure how much learner memory the smaller state saves
(E7.2 3.2). Both arms ran five synchronous updates on 32 training and eight inference H100s
in RNO, with the same seed and frozen recipe. Reduced-precision moments are class T: this
memory test informs a tradeoff and does not establish answer-quality equivalence. The
separate class X remainders replay still owns the byte-equality qualification.

**Results.** All ten original GPU tasks and both coordinators succeeded. An independent
Finelog query reproduced the collector's exact row hashes and its complete memory panel:
32 ranks, four phases, five updates, 480 measured phase exits per arm, and five distinct
once-per-node staging receipts per arm. There were no memory-threshold excursions.

| Measured quantity | Native optimizer | bf16 moments + remainders |
|---|---:|---:|
| Updates / seed | 5 / 17 | 5 / 17 |
| Optimizer state, bytes per owned parameter | 12.0 | 6.0 |
| Maximum optimizer state per rank, GiB | 23.427 | 11.714 |
| PPO peak allocated / reserved, GiB | 56.673 / 57.322 | 55.382 / 56.871 |
| Learner log-probability forward peak allocated, GiB | 53.817 | 42.102 |
| Weight-sync peak allocated / reserved, GiB | 58.099 / 61.732 | 46.387 / 56.090 |
| Model-ready allocated, GiB | 35.264 | 27.455 |
| Minimum device free at a phase exit, GiB | 7.569 | 4.771 |
| Sum of five core step intervals, seconds | 349.768417 | 354.990983 |
| Training duration p50, seconds | 6.136462 | 6.624321 |
| Weight-sync duration p50, seconds | 12.246959 | 11.580481 |
| Response tokens selected for training | 813,606 | 816,222 |
| Task GPU-hours, including startup and evaluation | 10.774180 | 10.960813 |
| Per-node dataset-ready to model-ready interval, seconds | 181.452–188.923 | 179.874–190.216 |
| Minimum fraction of exactly unit behavior ratios | 0.007578094489872456 | 0.007396275876089931 |
| Retained learner-to-learner maximum absolute log-ratio, every step | 0 | 0 |

Total task GPU-hours were **21.734993**. The native state inventory reports fp32 master,
first moment and second moment; the candidate reports int16 remainder storage and bf16
moments, rather than a resident fp32 master tensor. The state reduction is 6 bytes per
parameter. It does not translate directly into the same reduction in peak allocated memory
or device-free memory. These are single-seed memory observations; no confidence interval or
quality ranking is inferred from five updates. Completed correctness, semantic score and
truncation were not independently harness-audited here and are not reported as quality results.

The core interval is the frozen synchronous trainer's `step` span: generation through the
post-update weight sync, excluding callback evaluation, checkpointing and startup. Training
and sync medians use all five measured updates, including the first. These are the original
non-shard sync runner's timings; they are not measurements of the expert-block transport.
Token counts are the positive loss-mask response tokens, independently equal in the retained
generation-alignment, learner-monitor and age-zero mismatch counts at each update; all
1,629,828 selected tokens across the pair are age zero on that telemetry.

The CPU collector's two attempts both emitted identical complete results and then exited 1.
Its frozen pair verdict remains **FAIL**: the approved card and collector require the named
exact-unit fraction to equal 1.0, which neither arm meets. The failure is not a missing row,
failed native execution or memory exhaustion. It is a mismatch between the requested
identity check and the configured loss's ratio operand.

**What this means.** Both configurations satisfy the measured memory thresholds at 32
training GPUs. The behavior-clipped loss explicitly discards recomputed old learner log
probabilities and calculates its ratio from current training probabilities divided by vLLM
rollout probabilities. Synchronous policy versions do not require those different engines
to emit bitwise-equal probabilities. Its exact-unit fraction therefore cannot serve as the
intended learner-forward identity check. The collector reads that metric faithfully; its
interpretation as “sync C1 identity” is the defect. The same requirement occurs in the
approved design, so this audit does not silently replace it or claim its literal gate passed.

There is separate positive identity evidence already retained: the learner monitor compares
the actual training forward with recomputed old learner probabilities. At all five updates
in both arms its maximum absolute log-ratio is exactly zero, validity is 1, diagnostics-failed
is 0, and selected-token counts are positive. The update-index-zero monitor independently
agrees. This evidence is reported separately from the failed named behavior-ratio criterion.
A CPU counterexample reproduces exact learner identity with a behavior exact-unit fraction
of 0.5; changing the old learner operand leaves the behavior metric unchanged, and mutating
its denominator to the old learner operand makes the counterexample fail.

Neither arm is rejected for memory. The approved rule rejects allocated memory above 72 GiB
or device-free memory below 3 GiB only at the same phase exit on two of three repeats;
reserved-only excursions are remeasured with `expandable_segments`. Neither arm crossed any
of those limits, including the retained collector's diagnostic reserved threshold of 76 GiB.
The five updates and 32 ranks are not independent repeats. No memory repeat is triggered by
these observations, and a ratio failure cannot count as a memory repeat. This result alone
does not establish that 16 training GPUs fit or adopt the precision setting.

**Next.** Conclude the pair as an audited failure of the frozen named criterion, with the
memory and retained learner-identity subresults recorded as passing. Preserve the precision
choice for the measured gradient comparison and the smaller-learner evidence. The next
milestone is the learner-size decision. No GPU rerun is needed to collect or explain this
pair. A bounded CPU-only collector revision can expose separate `frozen_verdict`,
`memory_verdict`, `learner_identity_verdict` and `behavior_ratio_diagnostic` fields, retaining
the original receipt and all identity/coverage checks. It must not turn the frozen verdict
into PASS or relax a tolerance. A change to the approved named done-when belongs to Ahmad;
it does not hold unrelated queue work or prevent this failed group from concluding.

🤖 16 learner GPUs exhausted memory before completing 1 update with FP32 gradient reduction

**What we did and why.** We tested whether Snowball could use 16 learner GPUs and
24 inference GPUs, freeing more of the allocation for answer generation. The two
40-H100 runs compared expert-block weight sync with the full-broadcast reference,
using the same BF16 optimizer moments, parameter remainders and FP32 gradient
reduction. The precision package is class T; the transport is class X and still
requires its separate byte-equality and timing gate.

**Results.** Both runs reached the first rollout batch and failed inside the first
optimizer step while allocating Adam's first-moment state. The training progress
remained at 0 of 20 completed updates. These are scientific trainer-memory failures;
the later metrics-connection errors and gang teardown did not initiate the failures.

| Arm | Completed updates | Failed allocation | Device free at failure | PyTorch allocated at failure | PyTorch reserved but unallocated |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Expert-block sync | 0 | 14.00 MiB | 7.12 MiB | 61.86 GiB | 71.08 MiB |
| Full-broadcast reference | 0 | 14.00 MiB | 11.06 MiB | 62.68 GiB | 70.46 MiB |

These are the first exception's rounded memory snapshots, not phase-exit peaks or
whole-device PyTorch usage. Each device reported 79.18 GiB capacity; total process
usage including non-PyTorch memory was 79.17 and 79.16 GiB respectively. Each run
completed one rollout batch of 32 groups and 128 responses before training failed.
No trained-endpoint completed correctness, semantic score, confidence interval,
steady-state core time or 20-update transport result exists. Exact task GPU-hours
remain unknown because four of five gang tasks in each run lack a finish timestamp.

**What this means.** This frozen 16-learner recipe did not fit in either observed
run. The two scientific members are complete as audited failures, with no new
transport speedup or byte-equality claim. They are different transport arms, not
three identical repeats, so this result does not by itself satisfy the formal
repeat rule for rejecting every 16-learner configuration. The separately tested
BF16-gradient-reduction recipe retains its own result and identity.

**Next.** Combine this failure with the reduced-gradient recipe and the 32-learner
memory comparison to make the learner-size decision. Keep the working 32-learner
split for independent experiments while resolving that decision; no failed run is
silently retried or relabelled as the replacement.

🤖 BF16 gradient reduction still completed 0 updates on 16 Snowball learner GPUs

**What we did and why.** We tested the approved reduced-gradient recipe to see
whether Snowball could fit on 16 learner GPUs while leaving 24 GPUs for generation.
Both 40-H100 runs kept BF16 optimizer moments and parameter remainders, and compared
expert-block weight sync with the full-broadcast reference. The precision package is
class T; this run was also meant to provide the memory evidence for the smaller
learner split and qualify the class X transport at that geometry.

**Results.** Both runs reached training but exhausted device memory inside their
first optimizer step. The immediate failure was a BF16 optimizer-state conversion
to FP32 in FusedAdam. Each training progress log remained at 0 of 20 completed updates.

| Arm | Completed updates | Failed allocation | Device free at failure | PyTorch allocated at failure | PyTorch reserved but unallocated |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Expert-block sync | 0 | 14.00 MiB | 5.06 MiB | 62.32 GiB | 70.48 MiB |
| Full-broadcast reference | 0 | 14.00 MiB | 3.12 MiB | 62.63 GiB | 83.03 MiB |

The memory values are rounded snapshots from the first CUDA exception, not
phase-exit peaks. Each device reported 79.18 GiB capacity and 79.17 GiB process usage
including non-PyTorch memory. Each run completed one rollout batch of 32 groups and
128 responses before the failed update. The requested first-five-update memory row,
20-update byte-equality/timing row and trained-endpoint quality checks were not
produced. No quality interval or steady-state speed comparison is available. Exact
task GPU-hours are unknown because four sibling tasks per run lack finish timestamps.

**What this means.** Reducing gradient communication precision did not make this
frozen recipe fit in either observed run. These are scientific memory failures,
with the coordinator failures propagating the native result; staging and later
metrics-poller teardown errors are not the cause. Both declared scientific members
can close as audited failures. The result neither qualifies this topology nor
establishes a broad rejection under the identical-repeat memory rule: the two arms
use different transports. Startup transfer activity is not a substitute for the
missing update-level byte proof.

**Next.** Use the 32-learner memory results and these smaller-learner failures to
decide the next memory experiment, including the approved conditional alternative
backend if its prerequisite is met. Keep 32 learner GPUs as the working default
while making the learner-size decision. The conditional smaller-learner timing pair
still requires its recorded fit and prediction; this failed attempt does not supply
either.

🤖 No vLLM knob cleared both 5% speed tests; speculation acceptance was 19–33%

**What we did and why.** We audited the retained 16-arm Qwen vLLM knob sweep (E5.5), including its gang orphan, to identify generator settings that could support faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. The runs offered 128 requests per inference engine, with two control seeds and one seed for each changed setting. This closes the retained-evidence audit as an **operational evidence-contract failure**, with useful timing and speculation observations; it does not qualify an adopted setting or admit the orphan as a scientifically complete run.

**Results.**

The two speed columns and core seconds are arithmetic means over trainer updates 2–5, as frozen. The first speed metric counts **consumed** response tokens over the full cycle, not standalone generation capacity. Task GPU-hours include startup and shutdown according to controller attempt timestamps.

The 14 changed settings yielded **0 joint ≥5% speed candidates**, **12 with both absolute effects below 5%**, and **2 mixed outcomes** (sequence limit 16 and batched-token limit 2,048). The two control seeds differed by +0.66% and −3.97% on the respective speed metrics. None of these single-seed effects has a confidence interval; the control repeat is not a sampling distribution. All 16 arms reported zero request preemptions. Mean buffer-wait fractions over updates 2–5 were 0.134–0.177%, so consumed throughput must not be called inference capacity.

Controller-accounted cost was **27.6932 H100 GPU-hours** across 32 attempts: 25.9103 for the 15 ordinary arms and 1.7829 for the orphan. This is a sum of `8 × (attempt_finished_ms − attempt_started_ms) / 3,600,000`, never coordinator wall time. The orphan's worker ended with `PodDeleted`, so 1.7829 is controller-attempt accounting, **not verified physical allocation release**. CPU history, preflight and failed exception jobs contribute zero GPU-hours.

Stage-1 speculation counters, cumulative through update 6:

| Plain n-gram setting | Drafts | Draft tokens | Accepted tokens | Acceptance rate | Accepted draft tokens/draft | Mean emitted length including bonus |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| k=2, lookup max=3 | 343545 | 686746 | 225419 | 32.8242% | 0.6562 | 1.6562 |

| k=5, lookup max=4 | 294334 | 1467088 | 273235 | 18.6243% | 0.9283 | 1.9283 |

These are process-lifetime cumulative engine counters as sampled at update 6, not summed snapshots or isolated update-2–5 deltas. They may include startup evaluation and generation outside consumed training. Plain `ngram` disables async scheduling while the control retains it; therefore this is not a clean estimate of speculation's latency benefit. The Snowball stage-2 comparison is separately designed around `ngram_gpu`.

**What this means.** Retain the existing defaults: sequence limit 1,024, GPU memory utilization 0.75, batched-token limit 8,192, prefix caching on, speculation off. No class X/T setting is qualified by this audit. The speed-only threshold rejects 12 changed settings in this short measurement and leaves two conflicting results; the required reward veto is **not evaluable**, rather than passed or failed scientifically.

The reward defect affects the whole sweep, not just the orphan. All 15 recovered W&B histories lack `reward/avg_raw_reward` on updates 1–6, and their initial evaluation rows lack every step key accepted by the frozen reducer. The orphan's original stdout confirms the same namespace/cadence mismatch. Native N2 emits whole-cohort raw rewards as `async/cohort_preparation/reward/avg_raw_reward` only at steps 1, 3 and 5, while `loss/avg_final_rewards` describes each consumed partition. Substituting either into the registered per-update raw-reward check changes the statistic; no such substitution was made.

A second correction matters for work accounting: the manifest's “6 steps = 12 optimizer updates” is wrong for this runtime. The source requires exactly one successful optimizer update before each global-step advance; three cohorts × two partitions produce **six optimizer updates**. The orphan's Finelog rows independently report one successful valid optimizer update at every step 1–6. The frozen manifest is preserved as launch evidence.

**Next.** Stage-1 counter collection is complete and **unlocks Snowball speculation stage 2**, subject to its existing runtime and matched-packet checks. Compose the approved k=3/k=5/control comparison with `ngram_gpu`, raw logprobs and standard rejection sampling. This result does not adopt speculation. A future repair of the original reward/dump audit would need a reviewed scientific mapping and retained-object access; neither an identical CPU-audit retry nor a GPU rerun repairs the current evidence contract. The system-balance milestone can use this explicit failed-audit disposition and the stage-1 counters.

🤖 Sixteen inference GPUs used 23.4% more GPU-hours across 25 Snowball updates

**What we did and why.** The Snowball worker-split experiment (E5.2) compared P32/I8 with P32/I16 to identify an efficient allocation for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. Both runs used C1/A1/N1, seed 17, 32 prompts × four samples, and the shard synchronization path with proofs disabled. Each completed 25 updates; the first five were reserved for calibration and updates 6–25 for prediction validation.

**Results.**

| Successful original GPU tasks | 5/5 | 6/6 |
| Consumed loss/response tokens | 3,607,337 | 4,241,875 |
| Core seconds, all 25 updates | 955.647181 | 997.900548 |
| Mean core seconds/update | 38.225887 | 39.916022 |
| Core seconds, updates 1–5 | 216.376953 | 221.540670 |
| Core seconds, updates 6–25 | 739.270228 | 776.359878 |
| Cycle seconds | 957.839244 | 1,001.824993 |
| Whole task-allocation elapsed seconds¹ | 1,539.132 | 1,585.101 |
| Task H100 GPU-hours¹ | 17.079698 | 21.082847 |
| Consumed tokens/core second | 3,774.758167 | 4,250.799348 |
| Consumed training sequences | 3,200 | 3,200 |
| Training length stops | 132 (4.125%) | 223 (6.96875%) |
| Training stop-reason coverage | 100% | 100% |

² Optimization reward on consumed training sequences; this is not dev accuracy or a harness quality result.

³ Arithmetic mean of the 25 per-update ESS fractions, not a newly pooled token-level ESS.

The timer records have complete 25-update coverage:

| Timer, seconds summed across 25 updates | P32/I8 | P32/I16 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `run_training` | 238.99819250963628 | 244.2718119006604 |

The independently emitted phase windows give publication/core shares of 15.593625% / 16.944301%, buffer-wait/core shares of 58.762565% / 57.871811%, and training/core shares of 25.008399% / 24.477991% for I8/I16. Their window boundaries differ slightly from the named timers; do not interchange the numerators. Full shard install/freeze/finish and proof-timer decomposition was not audited.

| Recorded rollout outcome | I8 groups / tokens | I16 groups / tokens |
|---|---:|---:|
| Consumed | 800 / 3,607,337 | 800 / 4,241,875 |
| Stale at dequeue | 72 / 687,611 | 56 / 528,824 |

| Epoch discarded | 11 / 51,989 | 7 / 32,829 |

These are finalized rollout outcome counters. They do not establish complete engine-generated-token conservation, including unfinished or cancelled requests.

Evaluation failed before scoring. At the frozen runtime, `BasePPOExp.get_eval_dataset()` creates validation data only when `trainer.eval_interval > 0`; otherwise it returns `None`. Both envelopes set `eval_interval=-1`. The async driver skips evaluation when its dataset is `None`, even when the callback requests it. Consistently, the audited telemetry contains zero `eval/*` training metric rows and precisely initial publication plus 25 training publications per arm, with no evaluation publication. Expected dev input staging is present, but staging the input does not execute evaluation.

There is one run per arm, and no audited uncertainty interval or first-five-fit/remaining-twenty prediction result. The table is descriptive.

**What this means.** I16 used 23.4381% more task GPU-hours and 4.4214% more core time, while consuming 17.5902% more tokens. Its higher tokens/core-second rate therefore does not establish faster equal-work training, and the different consumed trajectories preclude treating this as a matched-reference timing pair. Keep the measurements, but leave the worker-split recommendation and the decision to close I16 undecided. The required evaluations and prediction validation remain unmet.

**Next.** Resolve the evaluation dataset guard and the missing native-dump-to-harness binding before making any quality statement. Complete the retained-counter throughput fit and its updates 6–25 validation before recommending an allocation for the system-balance milestone.

🤖 Snowball weight sync takes 5.76 s end to end with proofs off; transfer and install take 0.52 s

**What we did and why.** We measured the complete weight-sync interval to understand its remaining cost in faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. This proofs-off interval experiment (K10) ran Snowball 67B-A2B for 20 updates on 40 H100s: 32 Megatron policy GPUs (TP1/PP2/EP8) and 8 vLLM inference GPUs (DP8/EP8), on RNO. It used cadence 1, maximum age 1, one update per batch, seed 17, 32 prompts × 4 responses, 4,096 output tokens, 8,192 context tokens, learning rate 1e-6 and behavior clipping. We compared the durable phase receipts with native stdout, original task identities, completion evidence and Finelog; the earlier proofs-on pair supplies the full-byte qualification.

**Results.** All 20 updates and all five native tasks succeeded without a retry or preemption. Times below are seconds; the 95% intervals are exploratory within-run circular moving-block bootstrap intervals (block length 4, five blocks, 20,000 draws, seed 20260912). They describe this one sequential run and are neither between-seed uncertainty nor a paired speedup interval.

| Measured interval | Median | p95 | Median 95% interval | Sum over 20 |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| Whole weight sync | 5.756241 | 6.553578 | [5.539782, 5.952627] | 115.227924 |
| Transfer and install | 0.523978 | 0.897536 | [0.513145, 0.846215] | 13.104534 |
| Shard interval through finish | 4.101241 | 5.097784 | [3.802955, 4.349211] | 82.363226 |
| Training | 8.110999 | 12.782451 | [8.028609, 8.361779] | 199.965004 |
| Generation-buffer wait | 20.109141 | 40.395158 | [19.288945, 22.221253] | 458.979184 |
| Core | 34.008139 | 63.667365 | [33.385368, 36.022461] | 779.493197 |

The whole-sync median is **5.756240515504032 s**; the install median is **0.5239781602285802 s**. Whole sync includes pause, policy drains, the shard interval, resume and driver/control work. Install is the concurrent transfer-and-install RPC wall, reported as `timing/weight_broadcast`; it excludes the counter reads and the surrounding phases. The retained name `total_including_proof` denotes the shard interval through finish, **4.101240960415453 s median** here; both proof phases are absent. Initial preparation and initial sync are excluded from these 20 measured updates.

Generation-buffer wait is not identified as weight-related waiting. These measurements do not replace the outstanding proofs-subtracted, two-geometry analysis of the earlier matched pairs or settle the program's formal sync-plus-wait criterion.

The run consumed **2,989,994 loss tokens**, or **3,835.817956 tokens/core-second**. Cycle time summed to 818.881511 s. Exact native-task accounting is **7,151,711 / 450,000 = 15.89269111111111 GPU-hours**, summing eight GPUs times each task's own start-to-finish duration; core-only accounting is 8.661035517634202 GPU-hours. 🤖 Taking the newest queued rollouts first lowers mean age by 0.11–0.17 updates; answer-quality effects remain unknown

**What we did and why.** We tested whether changing which queued rollouts enter training can reduce their age without reducing prompt diversity, as a step toward faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. This admission-order experiment (E5.3) is **class T**: changing the selected training data can change the learning trajectory. On Qwen3-0.6B, we compared first-in-first-out (FIFO) with last-in-first-out (LIFO) at two matched seeds, and also tested freshest-first and age-weighted admission at one seed. Each run used eight learner and eight inference H100s for 96 updates, with 64 prompt groups and four responses per group per update, publication cadence four and maximum admitted age four updates.

**Results.**

All six runs completed their 96 updates. Age is the number of learner updates since generation of the first token; token mean weights each group's age by its consumed response-token count.

| Admission policy | Seed | Mean group age | Mean token age | Group / token age p95 | Stale groups discarded | Core seconds | Task H100-hours |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| FIFO | 17 | 2.458333 | 2.650071 | 4 / 4 | 0 | 559.999312 | 4.153762 |
| LIFO | 17 | 2.352214 | 2.240484 | 4 / 4 | 163 | 562.164481 | 4.033496 |
| Freshest-first | 17 | 2.341797 | 2.549011 | 4 / 4 | 179 | 567.203987 | 4.069702 |
| Age-weighted | 17 | 2.336589 | 2.372370 | 4 / 4 | 187 | 554.104825 | 4.034469 |
| FIFO | 29 | 2.458333 | 2.642055 | 4 / 4 | 0 | 561.758307 | 4.080498 |
| LIFO | 29 | 2.288411 | 2.174998 | 4 / 4 | 261 | 567.408816 | 4.178353 |

Against matched FIFO, LIFO lowered mean group age by 0.106120 and 0.169922 updates, and mean token age by 0.409587 and 0.467057 updates. Each run consumed 6,144 groups; all generated groups and response tokens reconciled to their terminal outcomes. Total allocation was 24.550280 H100-hours, calculated from actual task-attempt start and finish times. Core seconds cover the measured training core; allocation includes the rest of each task's lifetime. These are fixed-update observations on different trajectories, with no uncertainty intervals or quality-adjusted speedup established.

Every batch in every run contained 64 distinct canonical prompts. LIFO's relative diversity drop against FIFO was 0% at each matched seed, so the predeclared kill condition of a drop strictly greater than 20% did not fire.

The scientific quality comparison is incomplete. The retained evidence lacks harness records, the exact evaluation-pool and selection manifests, semantic scores, and held-out row-paired intervals. Native development aggregates were recorded at updates 0, 32, 64 and 96, but their original response dumps were not read in this audit; those aggregates are descriptive and cannot establish a quality winner.

**What this means.** LIFO reduced average consumed age in both matched seeds while preserving measured per-batch prompt diversity, but it discarded stale groups and did not reduce core time in either pair. Admission order remains undecided: there is no established answer-quality winner, no quality-preserving speedup, and no change to the default policy.

**Next.** Carry these scheduling measurements and the unresolved quality comparison into the system-balance analysis. Use the existing evaluation harness path to resolve the quality evidence before any admission-policy recommendation.

🤖 Speculative decoding saves only 0.523% of Snowball core time and worsens the slowest rollout groups

**What we did and why.** We tested whether proposing several tokens at once could deliver faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. This class T timing experiment compared speculation off with GPU n-gram proposals of three or five tokens. Each arm ran 25 updates with the same seed, 32 training GPUs and 8 inference GPUs, with native evaluations before and after training. The prespecified timing requirement was at least 10% improvement in both core time and rollout-group tail time.

**Results.** All three native arms completed their 25 updates successfully. Core time sums the training loop's measured core intervals; task GPU-hours include the full allocation of the five native tasks, including staging and evaluation.

| Arm | Core seconds | Change in core time | Task GPU-hours | Consumed response tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Speculation off | 4,894.817773 | Reference | 64.777171 | 3,759,171 |
| Three-token proposals | 4,934.755394 | 0.815916% slower | 65.326487 | 3,693,246 |
| Five-token proposals | 4,869.219389 | 0.522969% faster | 64.563913 | 3,311,280 |

Tail time is the gap between the first and last response finishing within a group of four responses. These quantiles describe the 800 consumed rollout groups in each arm; they are percentiles, not confidence intervals.

| Arm | Tail mean (s) | Tail p50 (s) | Tail p95 (s) | Tail p99 (s) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Speculation off | 13.835998 | 9.761425 | 35.080760 | 39.745393 |
| Three-token proposals | 15.658771 | 10.555822 | 41.185270 | 45.418646 |
| Five-token proposals | 14.354397 | 9.304171 | 42.115421 | 46.355922 |

Five-token proposals improved median tail time by 4.684301%, but worsened p95 by 20.052759% and p99 by 16.632189%. They consumed 11.914622% fewer response tokens while barely reducing core time, so this comparison does not establish a gain at matched output volume. Three-token proposals worsened core time and every reported tail summary.

Across the full process, including both native evaluations, three-token proposals accepted 1,766,802 of 11,381,223 drafted tokens (15.523833%); five-token proposals accepted 1,682,810 of 16,623,020 (10.123371%). These are differences of cumulative counters, not sums of repeated snapshots. Exact throughput per request is unavailable.

🤖 Parameter remainders save 2 bytes per parameter with exact agreement after 10 updates

**What we did and why.** We checked whether storing the low bits of each parameter can reduce optimizer memory while preserving the full-precision update, a class X (exact) lever toward faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. The update-ten remainders check (K14/K29) re-audited a retained native two-H100 execution of the actual Megatron/Transformer Engine optimizer on a synthetic 256 × 256 matrix. It compared FP32 optimizer moments plus 16-bit parameter remainders against the precision-aware FP32-master control, with the same FP32 gradients and moments. This required no new GPU allocation.

**Results.**

| Rank | Weight decay | FP32 master elements compared | BF16 model elements compared | Mismatched master / model elements |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 | 32,768 | 65,536 | 0 / 0 |
| 0 | 0.01 | 32,768 | 65,536 | 0 / 0 |
| 1 | 0 | 32,768 | 65,536 | 0 / 0 |
| 1 | 0.01 | 32,768 | 65,536 | 0 / 0 |

The native comparison covered every master and model bit: 262,144 bytes per rank/decay cell, or 1,048,576 compared bytes across the four cells, with 100% operand coverage. These are exhaustive checks of the retained operands, so a statistical confidence interval does not apply. All 20 embedded arm receipts matched their independently retained hashes, and every recorded gradient-shard oracle passed.

The remainders configuration retained 327,684 optimizer bytes per rank, versus 393,220 for the FP32-master control: exactly **2 bytes saved per owned parameter** in every cell. Both sides ran ten small-learning-rate updates at 1e-6, following a separate zero-gradient decay diagnostic at 1e-3. The original native execution used 0.084612 H100-hours; that historical allocation is reused as evidence and is not counted again.

**What this means.** Keep the exact remainders mechanism for this tested FP32-moment configuration. The broader combination with BF16 moments has a separate memory result; this comparison does not establish that BF16 moments reproduce FP32-moment arithmetic. At update ten the reconstructed masters moved, but the BF16 model changed-bit count was zero in every cell, so this is a mechanism proof rather than evidence of useful learning. It establishes neither Snowball/expert-parallel qualification, checkpoint resharding, nor answer-quality equivalence.

**Next.** Carry this scoped proof into the combined milestone on weight sync cut at least fourfold with bit-identical proof. Keep its optimizer-memory claim separate from the measured weight-sync speedup and the final quality comparison.

🤖 Standalone serving underpredicts training batch time by 19.1–26.0%

**What we did and why.** The inference-throughput study (E5.2) tested whether a controlled
serving measurement could predict training time and guide the policy-to-inference GPU ratio
for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. We ran one frozen
Qwen3-0.6B engine on one RNO H100 at requested concurrency 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256,
then fit `lambda_I(c) = lambda_max * c / (c + c_half)`. The audited collector used that curve
to re-predict batch time for four earlier trainer arms at their realised concurrency.
This is **class R research**: the ratio study decides whether the predictor supports a recommendation.

**Results.** All seven serving points passed their identity, steady-window and response checks.
The fit gave `lambda_max = 57,458.8` generated tokens/s/engine, `c_half = 106.34`, and maximum
absolute relative residual `0.128`.

| Requested c | Median running requests | Generated tokens/s |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 4.0 | 2,388.0 |
| 8 | 8.0 | 4,486.0 |
| 16 | 16.0 | 7,667.3 |
| 32 | 32.0 | 13,392.0 |
| 64 | 63.0 | 21,189.2 |
| 128 | 126.0 | 30,848.2 |
| 256 | 252.5 | 40,647.9 |

At the four trainer arms' realised concurrency, the resulting batch-time predictions were within
15% for **0/4 arms**. They underpredicted measured time by 19.1% to 26.0%. The same check at
nominal concurrency was also 0/4. None of the realised points was extrapolated below the sweep.

| Trainer setting | Realised requests per engine | Predicted batch s | Measured batch s | Prediction error |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 generation workers | 7.0000 | 11.023 | 14.897 | −26.0% |
| 128 generation workers | 9.0000 | 12.400 | 15.490 | −19.9% |
| 256 generation workers | 5.0625 | 12.381 | 15.459 | −19.9% |
| 256 generation workers, engine limit 16 sequences | 7.6875 | 13.192 | 16.315 | −19.1% |

Here a batch spans two optimizer updates; measured time is the median of the three batches
after the warm-up batch. These are single-run point estimates, with no confidence intervals.

**What this means.** The standalone curve fits the serving measurements, but its batch-time
predictions fail the training check. The Qwen ratio study closes as a negative result with
**no policy-to-inference ratio recommendation**. The standalone server and trainer used different
vLLM builds, and the model classified all four predictions as learner-bound, making the predicted
batch times insensitive to the tested inference concurrency. This check does not isolate the
cause of the prediction error or establish the trainer's actual bottleneck.

**Next.** Combine this negative result with the [completed Snowball ratio study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5649672543)
at the **system balance measured** milestone. Use native training measurements when choosing
the Snowball configuration for the final comparison.

🤖 Non-expert export takes 0.075 seconds in the two-layer probe

**What we did and why.** We decomposed weight export to find where further work could help faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. This observation supports the class X, exact-overlap investigation (K11): it measures the existing export path and changes no production behavior. A randomly initialized, Snowball-width model with two decoder layers ran through the real Megatron exporter and streaming bucket packer on two H100s in one node, with three parallelism/filter configurations. No weights were transferred to inference workers, and no training or answer evaluation ran.

**Results.**

| Export configuration | Exported tensors | Packed payload, GiB | Median export union, s | Observed range, s | Peak extra allocation, GiB |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| One pipeline stage, two expert partitions | 46 | 10.74 | 0.173 | 0.173–0.174 | 6.25 |
| Two pipeline stages, one expert partition | 46 | 10.74 | 1.682 | 1.005–2.359 | 7.81 |
| Two pipeline stages, non-expert tensors only | 40 | 1.37 | 0.075 | 0.074–0.075 | 0.61 |

Each row summarizes two ranks × two measured passes after one warm-up pass per rank. These are dependent observations from one allocation; the ranges are descriptive, not confidence intervals. Export union is the time covered by export CUDA-event spans, not a full synchronization interval or isolated kernel time. Packed bytes are not measured network traffic.

| Export configuration | Largest measured components | Median component share of export |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Two expert partitions | Expert gather | 63.5% |
| Two pipeline stages, all tensors | Pipeline tensor broadcast; object broadcast | 51.9%; 37.6% |
| Two pipeline stages, non-expert only | Conversion-task construction; pipeline tensor broadcast | 46.6%; 27.1% |

Shares are medians of the per-rank/pass ratios. The all-tensor pipeline configuration issued 1,058 tensor-broadcast calls and 524 object-broadcast calls per pass. The non-expert configuration selected 34 of 1,058 conversion tasks, while still paying the fixed cost of constructing the task list. Host waits for source-buffer release were measured separately: median 0.012 s, 0.013 s and 0.004 s in table order; they are not added to the contained export-component shares. Task GPU-hours were not reconciled in this observation receipt, and quality, consumed tokens and rollout age are not applicable.

**What this means.** Keep the decomposition as diagnostic evidence: export cost depends strongly on parallelism, and the non-expert remainder is small in this reduced model. It does not establish full-Snowball export latency, cross-node behavior, native overlap, receiver byte equality or a training speedup. The exact-overlap capability is not yet ready for adoption; this group closes only the observation probe.

**Next.** Preserve these measurements for choosing an overlap design after the final comparison runs have been launched. Work toward the final tradeoff statement remains ahead of this optional optimization; any later overlap candidate must demonstrate native overlap, byte equality and its measured effect on the full synchronization interval.

🤖 Partial-rollout version tagging fails the training-input identity check on 7 of 8 updates

**What we did and why.** We tested whether recording the policy version of each response segment preserves the training inputs when generation is interrupted and resumed (K18-D1 v2). These tags would help measure how old the data consumed by faster Snowball training actually is. This is a class X engineering change: its frozen gate requires identical consumed prompt-set digests and first-token admission-age summaries. We ran a control and tagged Qwen3-0.6B arm concurrently on RNO, each with 16 H100s, seed 17 and eight optimizer updates under an interruption-heavy configuration.

**Results.** Both jobs completed successfully, but the engineering identity gate failed.

| Check | Control | Version-tagged arm | Finding |
|---|---:|---:|---|

🤖 FP16 gradient scaling passes 3 finite updates and an injected overflow on 4 H100s

**What we did and why.** We qualified the native dense-gradient runtime needed to test lower-precision gradient reduction (E7.1b runtime qualification). This class T lever may reduce gradient storage and communication, but its quality and performance tradeoff must be measured before adoption for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. A synthetic diagnostic ran on four H100s on RNO with tensor parallelism 2 and data parallelism 2, using actual NCCL reduction, Transformer Engine backward and Adam, FP16 gradients and BF16 model parameters. We deliberately injected an overflow on one rank to check that every rank skipped the same update, reduced its loss scale and recovered together.

**Results.** All four ranks passed the same finite-update and overflow-recovery checks in one successful original task attempt.

| Optimizer attempt | Loss scale before → after | Update applied | Overflow observed | Result on all four ranks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 → 8 | Yes | No | Finite update |
| 2 | 8 → 16 | Yes | No | Finite update and scale growth |
| 3 | 16 → 8 | No | Yes, deliberately injected | Coherent skip and backoff |
| 4 | 8 → 8 | Yes | No | Finite recovery update |

The gradient buffer was FP16 at 131,072 bytes per rank throughout; model parameters remained BF16. The diagnostic checked exact finite parameter changes, FP32 master gradients and Adam moments, and a learning-rate scheduler that did not advance on the skipped update. This is a small synthetic layer, so its buffer size is not a production-model memory estimate.

| Potential benefit | Evidence here | Tradeoff still to measure |
|---|---|---|
| Lower gradient storage and communication | Native FP16 buffer/reduction path works on the tested dense topology | Full-model memory, step time and completed-answer quality are not measured by this group |
| Dynamic loss scaling | Growth, unanimous overflow skip/backoff and recovery pass | Unexpected non-finite training steps still trigger the scientific kill rule |

There is no held-out quality estimate, semantic score, consumed rollout count or confidence interval from this runtime diagnostic. The intentional overflow is a test condition, not a scientific training observation.

**What this means.** Keep the runtime available behind its opt-in flag for the separate gradient-precision comparison; it is not selected as the default. This qualification cleared a prerequisite for the full Qwen experiments, without qualifying their quality or production memory. The implementation remains limited to dense training with pipeline, expert and context parallelism each equal to 1; Snowball's expert/pipeline-parallel FP16 path and checkpoint/scaler restoration are unqualified.

**Next.** Complete the separate full-Qwen evidence and paired quality analysis to decide the precision tradeoff for the learner-size decision milestone. Any Snowball FP16 extension still needs its own implementation and qualification after the small-model scientific result; this kernel pass does not release it.
