spillover_issues.author: yonromai
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

On two H100 nodes connected through InfiniBand/GPU Direct RDMA, vLLM's
lossless sparse engine lifecycle was faster than dense at all 13 sampled
densities from 0% through 40% changed BF16 values. No sampled crossover
appeared.

On the 3.9045 GiB model-derived size-distribution proxy, the prior E6 anchors
measured:

- 8% changed / 92% unchanged: 161.45 ms sparse versus 354.50 ms dense, 2.20x
  faster and 193.05 ms saved.
- 14% / 86%: 185.65 ms versus 355.04 ms, 1.91x faster and 169.39 ms saved.
- 27% / 73%: 243.68 ms versus 357.63 ms, 1.47x faster and 113.95 ms saved.

At 40% changed / 60% unchanged, sparse took 305.07 ms versus 356.03 ms, a
1.17x speedup and 50.96 ms saved. Its 4.6854 GiB logical payload was already
larger than dense's 3.9045 GiB payload. The sparse communication component was
also slower, 118.40 ms versus 86.85 ms. The complete path still won because
dense application was much slower in this synthetic model. That is a dense
application-path result, not a wire advantage.

The data show no crossover at the sampled points. Under a monotonicity
assumption, the crossover is above 40% for this exact proxy and setup. They do
not establish a universal threshold or rule out an unexpected crossing between
samples.

## Description

A retained 20-step E6 run estimated 26.61% changed wire values after step 1,
13.68% on average, and 8.18% after step 20. Those are samples from one run, so
this experiment treats 8%, 14%, and 27% as anchors rather than a general RL
density distribution.

The source inventory is the public
[`marin-community/grug-67b-a2b-sft-s2-thinking-step630`](https://huggingface.co/marin-community/grug-67b-a2b-sft-s2-thinking-step630)
safetensors index at revision
`6808fe5c219471517bd51df35addefd38ebebf89`: 502 BF16 tensors,
67,078,882,816 values, and 134,157,765,632 bytes. The benchmark preserves all
502 entries while dividing each flattened element count by 32. The timed proxy
has 2,096,215,088 BF16 values and 4,192,430,176 bytes (3.9045 GiB).

This is a size-distribution proxy, not a target-model installation. It flattens
the entries into one synthetic `ParameterList`, renames them `tensor_0` through
`tensor_501`, and uses vLLM's `default_weight_loader`. It does not preserve the
model's shapes, hierarchy, expert mappings, packed mappings, or custom loaders.
The scale-down can move the crossover density, not merely reduce absolute time,
because fixed per-tensor and application work do not scale like payload bytes.

For `N` BF16 values and changed fraction `d`, dense sends about `2N` bytes.
Sparse sends about `6dN` bytes for one `int32` index and one BF16 replacement.
The one-third raw-byte boundary is separate from the complete time crossover,
which includes detection, packing, control metadata, communication,
synchronization, and receiver application.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Answer this narrow question using the installed vLLM engine implementations:

> On the tested two-node H100 InfiniBand setup and model-derived tensor-size
> proxy, at which sampled change densities does sparse beat dense, and by how
> much?

The experiment compares dense and sparse update lifecycles in one allocation,
keeps full-byte checks outside the timed interval, and records component time,
logical payload, effective bandwidth, and peak additional GPU memory.

## Status

Complete. Final Iris job
[`/romain/sparse-crossover-2n-v7-01a098b0`](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/job/%2Fromain%2Fsparse-crossover-2n-v7-01a098b0)
succeeded with 2/2 tasks, zero failures, and zero preemptions in 2m59s.

The run used two leaf-group-coscheduled `H100x8` node allocations on
`cw-rno2a` at interactive priority, with CUDA device 0 used on each host. The
hosts were `g779de0` and `g830782`. NCCL reported two ranks on two nodes, all
eight 400 Gb/s `ibp` devices per host, GPU Direct RDMA, and channels using
`NET/IB/0/GDRDMA`.

Each density used two warmups followed by five latency samples. The warmups'
CUDA allocator state was retained. Complete latency is the slower sender or
receiver time for each repetition, then the median. Dense and sparse order
alternated by density. CUDA synchronization surrounds timed work. Model reset
and full-byte comparison are outside the timed interval. Peak memory is
measured separately in one allocator-cold pass, so cache release does not
invalidate the warmed latency result. Raw evidence retains every sample.

The two-node path invokes installed
`NCCLTrainerWeightTransferEngine.send_weights` and `NCCLWeightTransferEngine`
start/update/finish for dense, and the corresponding installed sparse trainer
and receiver methods for sparse. Sparse detection and packing occur inside the
timed sender operation. Names, shapes, dtypes, and changed counts cross a local
two-rank Gloo control shim as the same serialized dictionaries expected by
`VLLMWeightSyncClient`; acknowledgements are timed. This excludes HTTP/Ray/API
queuing and a live serving process, but includes installed engine metadata,
validation, NCCL, synchronization, and receiver application. At 0%, detection
is timed before the installed sparse trainer treats the empty patch list as a
no-op.

The full sweep was:

- 0% changed / 100% unchanged: 26.70 ms sparse versus 364.34 ms dense, 13.64x.
- 0.01% / 99.99%: 147.69 ms versus 355.48 ms, 2.41x.
- 0.1% / 99.9%: 151.62 ms versus 356.97 ms, 2.35x.
- 0.5% / 99.5%: 153.51 ms versus 355.18 ms, 2.31x.
- 1% / 99%: 153.52 ms versus 355.21 ms, 2.31x.
- 2% / 98%: 153.35 ms versus 354.92 ms, 2.31x.
- 5% / 95%: 157.86 ms versus 355.25 ms, 2.25x.
- 8% / 92%: 161.45 ms versus 354.50 ms, 2.20x.
- 14% / 86%: 185.65 ms versus 355.04 ms, 1.91x.
- 20% / 80%: 211.78 ms versus 354.26 ms, 1.67x.
- 27% / 73%: 243.68 ms versus 357.63 ms, 1.47x.
- 33% / 67%: 270.28 ms versus 354.62 ms, 1.31x.
- 40% / 60%: 305.07 ms versus 356.03 ms, 1.17x.

The fastest dense sample was slower than the slowest sparse sample at every
density. At 40%, the conservative observed gap was 49.07 ms.

All 13 points produced byte-identical dense, sparse, and target weight images
across all 4,192,430,176 receiver bytes. Each untimed check repeats the same
installed trainer/receiver lifecycle and serialized metadata path used for
timing. This proves the tested weights only; it does not prove live-serving
scheduler, KV-cache, or inference correctness. The
one-GPU companion
[`/romain/sparse-crossover-1g-v5-final-01a098b0`](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/job/%2Fromain%2Fsparse-crossover-1g-v5-final-01a098b0)
also passed every density and a packed/TP-style loader smoke.

The one-GPU p90 probe exposed the current patch loader's full-shape temporary.
For one changed entry in an 838,860,800-value BF16 tensor (1.5625 GiB), it
allocated 2.3438 GiB extra. A zero-entry patch was essentially the same. This is
a current implementation cost, not an inherent sparse requirement.

Both final ranks independently installed the exact qualified release artifact:

- [vLLM CUDA 13.2 release](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20260912-177d960f5b43)
- source commit: `177d960f5b437a813738b1d9544f150ba41dc200`
- wheel: `vllm-0.0.0.dev20260912+marin.177d960f5b43.cu132-cp38-abi3-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl`
- wheel SHA-256: `93684330f606a830417431bf29b7cb47498d9ed723f86ed64694ee7b5d21c655`
- constraints SHA-256: `2efc99bedebabc6921ea369e524637f7ee1d6da39c23289075599d5433a71dcc`
- task image: `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task@sha256:9af9a3d38f57c2ed8dfe1d6f6657a9f4a00c582ec06a5ac2af8fcddbe51da03c`
- Torch 2.13.0+cu132, CUDA 13.2, NCCL 2.29.7

The two complete installation records are byte-identical with SHA-256
`cdc240b1428f9d804a7afaa7e36ce8db71cb090c282c1b1f6e262c4f983401bc`.

To reproduce, download the files from the exact Gist revision into one
directory. From a Marin checkout whose Iris CLI can reach `cw-rno2a`, run:

```bash
marin-env uv run --package marin-iris python /path/to/bundle/submit_benchmark.py one-gpu \
  --name-suffix reproduce-1g-YYYYMMDD
marin-env uv run --package marin-iris python /path/to/bundle/submit_benchmark.py two-node \
  --name-suffix reproduce-2n-YYYYMMDD
```

The submitter resolves the bundle relative to its own file. It no longer
depends on the author's private session path.

## Links

- [Exact public evidence and reproduction bundle](https://gist.github.com/yonromai/5877a918242fa96ff6109c9233b733a5/60ae8b94abe22266ca80dff2a77d476d4a8cbe7f)
- [Raw two-node JSON](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/yonromai/5877a918242fa96ff6109c9233b733a5/raw/5bb4273c45450cfec621bfdace8ce15833da73a1/sparse-crossover-two-node.json), SHA-256 `a154496815f9fe759eebd8dc1c9a6fa77e94db170a7cd192417bdbbe26b4d663`
- [Benchmark source](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/yonromai/5877a918242fa96ff6109c9233b733a5/raw/22edc05e0c0a76b273cd22f12011850c69fbb938/sparse_crossover_benchmark.py), SHA-256 `50080073f49f4b54ce432419353a2549d4c54bb466dfcf469585900fe783335f`
- [Submitter](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/yonromai/5877a918242fa96ff6109c9233b733a5/raw/b2843467b894cb7d4b7509e670f69d2286a53526/submit_benchmark.py), SHA-256 `27b19e9ddf32d82a735c6779093cda2d7666644b16a4554e8bf5cb8b7f543d51`
- [Bounded NCCL path evidence](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/yonromai/5877a918242fa96ff6109c9233b733a5/raw/0d905bcaca1a2c24923e71c345cbe52d3d128921/nccl-path-evidence.txt)
- Related dense-publication work: #8955
- Pending linearization: [marin-community/vllm#56](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/56)

## Decision Log

- Used a 32x element-scaled, 502-entry model-derived size proxy so complete
  lifecycle samples and every-byte checks fit on one H100. The issue does not
  extrapolate its times or crossover density to the full checkpoint.
- Used a scattered pattern. Every positive density changes at least one value
  in every tensor, retaining 1,004 small-message index/value broadcasts.
- Separated warmed latency from allocator-cold peak memory after final review
  found that cache release between repetitions invalidated the original warmed
  claim.
- Replaced direct data-plane calls in the complete timer with installed trainer
  and receiver engine methods plus serialized control payloads after review
  found that metadata and lifecycle work were missing.
- A focused re-review then found two residual gaps. The final harness times
  detection at 0% before the engine no-op and repeats the installed engine path,
  including serialized metadata, for every untimed equality check.
- A pre-final attempt found Gloo selecting an unreachable interface, so the
  harness pins it to `enp90s0np0`. Another attempt exposed a report merge bug
  that discarded rank 0's component dictionary. Both were corrected before the
  final `v7` result.
- Stopped at the required point above the 33% byte boundary because no sampled
  timing crossover appeared. The issue reports the bounded observation rather
  than extrapolating an unmeasured crossover.
- At publication, vLLM PR #56 remained open at `4c1c798a`. No release newer
  than the pinned artifact contained a CUDA 13.2 wheel. The newer
  `6cf1de831b68` release is CUDA 12.9 from a separate history and does not
  contain the sparse engine or patch loader, so it is not the linearized
  replacement and the requested replacement-wheel smoke does not apply yet.
  Reuse this result only after comparing a future CUDA 13.2 replacement's
  sparse engine, patch loader, and dependency closure with the pinned artifact.
- No MarinSkyRL or vLLM source, dependency, lock, or configuration was changed.

## Conclusion

Sparse beats dense at every tested point, including the 8–27% E6 anchors, on
this two-node H100 InfiniBand setup and scaled size-distribution proxy. The
result supports one smaller integration experiment, but does not measure a
complete MarinSkyRL publication pause, asynchronous RL throughput, live-serving
correctness, or eight-way tensor-parallel fan-out.

The smallest next experiment is a shadow-only encoder on one retained E6 weight
pair and a disposable live vLLM receiver. Form the exact per-rank BF16 views
already sent to rollout workers, record changed counts and encode time, exercise
the normal API lifecycle, compare fixed-prompt inference after dense and sparse
installation, require full-byte equality, and compare the adaptive choice
without changing live publication or training semantics.

## Final result

Changing the router input to the existing gated latent did not improve Paloma
loss or expert load balance in these two single-seed comparisons. Both corrected
treatments completed; no larger cells or new baselines were launched.

Idea credit: **Zihan Qiu**. Controls are Larry's completed **LatentMoE + RMSNorm +
GatedNorm** TPU experiments in #6822.

```text
Reference: h → router; down(h) → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → routed experts
Treatment: down(h) → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → router + routed experts
```

| Width | Updates | Tokens, each run | Reference Paloma | Treatment Paloma | Treatment − reference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| d512 | 10,980 | 1,439,170,560 | 3.570037 | 3.569422 | −0.000615 |
| d768 | 16,875 | 4,423,680,000 | 3.214935 | 3.219741 | +0.004806 |

d512 is effectively tied; d768 is slightly worse. A single seed per cell does
not establish statistical significance.

Load-balance statistics average exactly the final 100 training steps, aligned
between treatment and reference. Higher routing entropy is more uniform; the
load-balancing loss below is a diagnostic, not an optimized auxiliary loss.

| Width | Entropy, reference → treatment | Load-balancing diagnostic, reference → treatment | Overflow, both |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| d512 | 5.525794 → 5.519022 | 4.089624 → 4.152348 | 0 |
| d768 | 5.530514 → 5.525864 | 4.060266 → 4.092398 | 0 |

Both treatments are slightly less balanced, mainly in the first layer. All
runs remain close to uniform usage of 256 experts.

The corrected launcher uses **GrugMoeMuonHConfig**: GatedNorm and other matrices
use MuonH, router and norm scales use Adam, and lm_head uses AdamH. Uploaded live
config artifacts confirm `grug_moe_muonh_v1`. The original September identities
without `-muonh` used the wrong optimizer and remain invalid for this comparison.

The matched recipe preserves Larry's MLA architecture, gate/expert path,
initialization recipe, cached data, batch, schedule and evaluation protocol.
Current runtime dependencies differ from July. Last-100-step throughput was
339,590 → 342,765 tokens/s at d512 and 221,056 → 225,086 at d768
(reference → treatment); these are descriptive measurements, not controlled
speedups. The historical analytic FLOP logger is not validated for MLA/latent.

Both Iris parents and children succeeded and W&B reports finished. d768

## Previous attempt (comparison withdrawn)

The earlier September hero-shape treatments completed, but their May references
were not matched controls. Their large loss gap does not establish a causal
regression from gated routing. The unsubmitted H100 ladder rerun is superseded.

<details>
<summary>Historical experiment description and results (superseded)</summary>

## Description

The current EP hero routes the full-width pre-MLP feature `h`; its routed experts receive `RMSNorm(down(h))`. This experiment changes the path to:

```python
u = RMSNorm(h @ W_latent_down)
z = u * sigmoid(silu(u @ W_gate_down) @ W_gate_up)
router_logits = z @ W_router
routed_output = combine(selected_experts(z)) @ W_latent_up
```

The second line is the existing `GatedNorm` class. RMS normalization is a separate operation immediately before that gate. Both the gate and the router read the normalized latent path, and the routed experts receive `z`.

The latent RMSNorm and its learned scale remain trainable. Router gradients flow through the gate, RMSNorm and latent down projection. Router input width changes from hidden width to latent width. Shared experts continue to read `h`; outer norms, QB load balancing, sigmoid combine weights and the shared latent up projection retain the hero behavior.

This tests the combined change of adding the latent gate and routing on its output. It does not separate the contribution of those two changes.

Acknowledgment: **Zihan Qiu proposed this idea.**

User request (verbatim):
> ok准备一个ablation，把latent down之后的norm改成gated norm，然后把router input换成这个gated norm之后的feature，然后follow agent moe ablate一下（acknowledge Zihan Qiu  for the idea in the issue)

Architecture clarification:
> down(h) → RMSNorm → gate → router + experts
>
> 我指的是这个

## Hypothesis or Goal

Routing on the same gated normalized feature consumed by the experts may improve expert specialization and loss enough to offset the gate's runtime cost.

Follow the Agent MoE gates, training only the treatment:

| Gate | Hidden width | Reference FLOP budget | Corrected run ID |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 512 | 3.82e17 | `moe-lgr-9110-d512-rmsgated` |
| 1 | 768 | 2.81e18 | `moe-lgr-9110-d768-rmsgated` |
| 2, conditional | 1024 | 1.16e19 | `moe-lgr-9110-d1024-rmsgated` |
| 2, conditional | 1280 | 3.46e19 | `moe-lgr-9110-d1280-rmsgated` |

Reuse `moe_may_compute_opt_d{dim}_ep1` in `marin-community/marin_moe`. **Do not submit new baseline jobs.** The control implementation exists only for numerical parity tests and analytic schedule calculation.

Gate 1 requires effective speedup above 1 at both small widths. Only then run Gate 2, which requires improvement at all four widths and lower projected loss at 1e21 and 1e23 FLOPs. Use the guide's recentered scaling comparison with exponent 0.0941 and asymptote 1.6.

Record final Paloma macro loss, total tokens, mean throughput over the last 100 training steps, routing statistics, successful Iris completion, W&B `finished` and final checkpoint metadata. Report actual analytic compute and compute-equivalent gain separately from the wall-clock comparison, using each run's own token count and throughput. The historical references use a different recipe and v4-32 hardware; this scaled hero treatment uses v5p-8. Those differences limit attribution of any gain to this intervention.

Prior work: #8105 tested a dynamic latent projection while retaining RMSNorm. It did not test the shared RMSNorm-then-gate routing feature proposed here.

## Status

Both RMSNorm-before-gate runs in the first, small-model experiment stage (Gate 1) completed successfully on September 12: d512 Iris attempt 3 and d768 attempt 2 exited 0, and both W&B runs are finished. Permanent checkpoint metadata is verified at steps 13,642 and 19,378. Routing overflow remained zero and recorded metrics were finite. Source: `edf9b2871`; architecture: `down(h) -> RMSNorm -> gate -> router + routed experts`. Idea: **Zihan Qiu**.

| Hidden width | Treatment Paloma loss | Reference Paloma loss | Tokens, treatment / reference | Last-100 mean tokens/sec, treatment / reference | Treatment non-embedding training FLOPs | Recentered compute ratio | Effective speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 512 | 3.84245491 | 3.54216671 | 1,788,084,224 / 1,439,170,560 | 340,373.87 / 431,263.12 | 3.798955e+17 | 0.217010 | 0.137854 |
| 768 | 3.55822515 | 3.22727251 | 5,079,826,432 / 4,423,680,000 | 200,154.66 / 291,668.98 | 2.798080e+18 | 0.139819 | 0.083556 |

The numerical comparison against historical references is below 1 at both widths, but it is not a matched ablation and cannot establish a gate failure. No d1024/d1280 runs or Gate 2 scaling fit will be launched. No additional baseline or smoke was run.

Using the [Agent MoE guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/moe-latent-gated-router/experiments/grug/moe/agent.md) scaling-law assumption (loss asymptote 1.6, exponent 0.0941), the compute ratio is `((L_reference - 1.6)/(L_treatment - 1.6))**(1/0.0941)`. Effective speedup is a model-based estimate, not a measured acceleration. It divides the estimated reference time to reach the treatment loss (`compute_ratio * reference_tokens / reference_TPS`) by treatment time (`treatment_tokens / treatment_TPS`). TPS is the mean of exactly the last 100 training steps. These times exclude queueing, preemption, compilation, evaluation and checkpoint overhead. Analytic non-embedding training FLOPs are `3 * (forward_FLOPs_per_token - 2*hidden_dim*vocab_size) * treatment_tokens`; they are distinct from the loss-derived compute ratio.

The reused May references use a different architecture, optimizer/data recipe and v4-32 hardware; treatment uses the [scaled hero latent configuration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/moe-latent-gated-router/experiments/grug/moe_latent_gated_router) on v5p-8. This comparison does not isolate the causal effect of adding the gate or changing router input.

- 2026-09-11: User instruction: “别smoke浪费卡了，直接跑”. Cancel the pending corrected smoke and directly launch the two full variants.

## Conclusion

### Comparison correction — September 12

The May reference is not a matched control for this ablation. The previous Gate 1 failure wording must not be interpreted as evidence that RMSNorm-then-gate routing hurts quality. The measured losses remain valid for these runs, but the ablation conclusion is inconclusive.

Actual W&B configuration differences include 256/top-4 versus 384/top-8 experts, a full-width MoE versus the hero latent bottleneck, different shared-expert structures, optimizer beta1 0.9062 versus 0.9, minimum LR ratio 0 versus 0.05, different learning rates and token budgets, and training z-loss weight 0 versus 1e-4. Evaluation batch size is 512 in the references versus 32/64 in treatment, with max_eval_batches=8 in both, so the evaluation sample budgets also differ. Hardware is v4-32 versus v5p-8; the estimated speedups do not isolate architectural efficiency.

Tokenizer identity is the same (`meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B`), and named training-source mixture weights agree after removing the treatment's `-llama3` suffix. Cache identity and exact evaluation examples have not been established as equivalent. Different cache paths alone do not prove different source data.

No new runs are being launched. A valid gate ablation needs a reference with the same hero architecture, training recipe, and evaluation protocol, differing only in the intended gate/router intervention. Until such a matched existing reference is found or a new comparison is explicitly agreed, no causal pass/fail conclusion is warranted. Idea credit remains Zihan Qiu.

### Existing baseline search — September 12

Located the hero-shape scaling-ladder references:
- d512: [h100-ladder-d512-ep8-bs1024-791tpp-20260824-rno2a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/h100-ladder-d512-ep8-bs1024-791tpp-20260824-rno2a), 16,483,614,720 tokens, batch 1024.
- d768: [h100-ladder-d768-2xep8-bs1024-791tpp-20260824](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/h100-ladder-d768-2xep8-bs1024-791tpp-20260824), 47,898,951,680 tokens, batch 1024. A batch-512 sibling also exists.

These share the 384/top-8, hidden/2 latent and expert widths, two shared experts, 6/8 layers, SConv k/attn/mlp, HIST QB with 10k bins, and capacity 1.15 configuration. However, they use the Harrier mixture, top-level Marin tokenizer setting, H100 pooled EP transport, different LR/beta2, and different evaluation budgets. Treatment used the Agent MoE Nemotron/StarCoder/ProofPile recipe with the Llama-3.1 tokenizer setting and batch 32/64 on v5p-8. The ladder's evaluation cache names contain `-llama3`; actual cache-tokenizer equivalence requires further verification, so tokenizer config differences alone should not be interpreted as proven evaluation-token differences.

Completed filtered W&B searches across `marin_moe`, `marin_moe_ragged`, `grug_latent_ablation`, and `qbb_latentmoe_ringEP` for hidden width 512/768, 384 experts, top-8, sequence length 4096, and the treatment's exact top-level tokenizer setting returned only the two treatment runs and the superseded smoke. No matched existing control was found in that scope. Issue #8227 and #8105 baselines use 192/top-4 and are excluded.

The original experiment combined the hero architecture with a different training recipe instead of matching one of these existing hero baselines. To reuse an existing baseline, the treatment must be aligned to its full configuration and schedule. The completed treatment runs cannot currently support a controlled gate comparison. No new training was launched during this search.
